title: Supreme Court: 2025 civil services allocation must follow its OBC creamy-layer ruling
dek: The court refused the Centre two years to settle how private and public-sector posts compare, gave it two months to comply, and said past selections will not be reopened.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Supreme Court on Friday refused to shield this year's civil services allocations from its March ruling on the OBC creamy layer, directing that the services of candidates selected in the 2025 Civil Services Examination be allotted under its stricter reading of who counts as "creamy layer".

A bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and R. Mahadevan rejected the Centre's request for two years to work out how posts in public-sector companies, banks and private firms compare with government posts, and gave the government two more months to comply with the March judgment. It also said that selections and appointments completed before that judgment will not be reopened merely because of it.

## What the court said

The Centre had filed applications asking the court to clarify its judgment of 11 March in Union of India v Rohith Nathan. That ruling held that a parent's salary alone cannot decide whether an Other Backward Classes candidate falls in the creamy layer, which is excluded from reservation, and that the status and category of the parent's post must also be considered.

In Friday's order the court said "miscellaneous applications cannot be employed as a means to seek a rehearing of matters already decided". Its main directions were:

- The March judgment settles the rights of the parties, and the candidates who challenged their exclusion are non-creamy-layer OBC.
- Granting them the benefit does not, by itself, harm the seniority of others or reopen concluded selections.
- The government may accommodate eligible candidates, in line with an assurance from the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) that supernumerary posts can be created.
- Selections and appointments concluded before 11 March 2026 are not to be reopened on the strength of the judgment alone.
- Selections and roster allotments made after 11 March are governed by the 1993 government order as the court interpreted it.
- For CSE-2025, service allocation for OBC candidates shall follow the creamy-layer principle as interpreted in March.
- No timeline is prescribed for the government to establish equivalence of posts or frame a creamy-layer policy, so the request for two years "does not arise".

"The time for compliance with the judgment is extended by a period of two months from today," the court said, which takes the deadline to early January 2027.

## Background

The creamy-layer rules come from an office memorandum issued in 1993, after the Supreme Court's Indra Sawhney judgment upheld OBC reservation but said the better-off among them should be excluded. A 2004 clarification allowed parents' salaries to be counted where the equivalence of a post in a public-sector company, bank, university or private firm with a government post had not been settled. The court held in March that this clarification could not add a condition that was not in the 1993 policy, and that treating children of public-sector or private employees differently could breach the right to equality.

The Union Public Service Commission declared the CSE-2025 final result on 6 March, recommending 958 candidates for the IAS, IPS, Indian Foreign Service and other central services, reports said. The judgment came five days later, and service allocation was held up while the Centre sought clarification. The Centre argued that applying the ruling retrospectively could unsettle appointments and admissions made over years; one report said the 1993 framework had been used to fill more than 5.69 lakh reserved vacancies between 2016 and 2025. The court reserved its decision on 24 September.

## What happens next

The DoPT must now complete CSE-2025 service allocation under the court's reading of the creamy-layer rules, within two months. OBC candidates who were treated as creamy layer under the salary test could have their status reassessed, one report has said. Because the court left the equivalence of posts without a deadline, the government's wider creamy-layer policy for public-sector and private-sector employees' children remains to be framed.
